config.title: Error handling

intro.title: Error handling
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Express server that gracefully handles errors when a user tries to access a non-existent route. You will learn the core concept of error handling by using Express middleware to catch and respond to errors. The main technologies involved are the Express framework and JavaScript's built-in error objects. You'll implement a custom error handler to return a user-friendly JSON response instead of a default HTML error page.
intro.usecase: Error handling is essential in any production Express application to provide clear feedback when things go wrong. In e-commerce platforms, proper error handling ensures users see helpful messages when payment processing fails or inventory is unavailable. API services use structured error responses to help client applications understand issues like invalid authentication or rate limiting. Without robust error handling, users encounter confusing crashes instead of actionable information to resolve lessons.

objectives: Implement a basic error handler middleware function in an Express application
Configure Express to serve custom error pages for different HTTP status codes
Construct a centralized error handling function to process and respond to errors
Apply try-catch blocks to asynchronous route handlers to catch operational errors
Integrate a global error handler at the end of the Express middleware chain
Manipulate error objects to include custom properties for debugging and logging
Initialize a custom Error class to extend built-in error functionality

steps.title: Import Express and create error handling middleware
steps.instruction: Import the Express library and create a basic error handling middleware function that logs errors to the console and sends a generic 500 status response.
steps.hint: Use require('express') to import Express. Create a function with parameters (err, req, res, next) that logs the error and sends a response.
steps.seedCode: // Import Express and create error handling middleware here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have Express imported and a middleware function ready to handle errors.
successCriteria: Express is imported using require(), and an error handling middleware function is created with proper parameters that logs errors and sends a 500 response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have both the Express import and a function with (err, req, res, next) parameters that logs errors and sends a response.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're importing Express with require() and creating a function that handles errors by logging and sending a 500 response.

steps.title: Create a basic Express server with routes
steps.instruction: Create an Express server with a few basic routes (GET /, GET /users, etc.)
steps.hint: Initialize an Express app, define routes using app.get(), and start the server listening on a port.
steps.expectedOutcome: A minimal Express server with at least two GET routes defined and the server listening on a port.
successCriteria: Express app is created with app.get() routes for '/' and '/users' (or similar), and app.listen() starts the server.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both routes defined (e.g., '/' and '/users') and the server is started with app.listen().
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created the Express app, defined at least two GET routes, and started the server with app.listen().

steps.title: Add a route that intentionally throws an error
steps.instruction: Add a GET route at '/error' that throws a new Error with the message 'Something went wrong'.
steps.hint: Use app.get() with '/error' as the path and a handler function that throws new Error('Something went wrong').
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will have a route that intentionally triggers an error when visited.
successCriteria: A GET route at '/error' exists and throws a new Error with message 'Something went wrong'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the route is at '/error' and throws a new Error with the exact message 'Something went wrong'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route isn't set up correctly. It should be a GET route at '/error' that throws a new Error.

steps.title: Test the error without error handling middleware
steps.instruction: Start the Express server by adding the app.listen() call with port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen() with port 3000 and a console.log to indicate the server is running.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will start successfully, allowing you to test the error route in the next step.
successCriteria: The server starts without errors and logs a message to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added app.listen(), but make sure it includes both the port and a callback function that logs a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've called app.listen() with port 3000 and a callback that logs a message to the console.

steps.title: Register the error handling middleware
steps.instruction: After your routes, add the error handling middleware function to the Express app using app.use().
steps.hint: Place app.use() after your routes but before app.listen(). The middleware function should be passed as an argument to app.use().
steps.expectedOutcome: The error handling middleware is registered in the Express app after the routes.
successCriteria: app.use() is called after the routes and before app.listen(), with the error handling middleware function as its argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure app.use() is placed after the routes and before app.listen(). Also, ensure you pass the error handling middleware function as the argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handling middleware is not correctly registered. Check that you're using app.use() after the routes and passing the middleware function as an argument.

steps.title: Test error handling with the middleware
steps.instruction: Inside the '/error' route handler, throw a custom error with a descriptive message.
steps.hint: Use the JavaScript throw statement with a new Error object containing a message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The '/error' route will now throw a custom error when accessed, which will be caught by your error handling middleware.
successCriteria: The '/error' route handler contains a throw statement with a new Error object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the throw statement with new Error('message') inside the route handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route handler doesn't contain a proper error throw. Remember to use throw new Error('message') inside the function.

steps.title: Create an asynchronous route that throws an error
steps.instruction: Create a new route handler for the '/async-error' endpoint that uses async/await and throws an error asynchronously.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the route handler function, then throw an error inside an async context.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will have a new '/async-error' route that uses async/await and throws an error when accessed.
successCriteria: A new route handler for '/async-error' is created with the async keyword and throws an error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your route handler uses the async keyword and actually throws an error. Check the syntax of your async function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route handler doesn't seem to be implemented correctly. Remember to use async/await and throw an error inside the handler.

steps.title: Test asynchronous error handling
steps.instruction: Start your Express server by running `node app.js` in your terminal,
steps.hint: Make sure your server is running before testing the route. Check the terminal for any server startup messages.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see that the async error might not be caught properly by your current error handling middleware, resulting in an unhandled promise rejection or incomplete response.
successCriteria: Observed that error isn't properly caught
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the server, but make sure to actually test the /async-error route to see how async errors behave.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server needs to be running and the async error route tested to observe the error handling behavior.

steps.title: test the async error route by visiting http:/
steps.instruction: test the async error route by visiting http://localhost:3000/async-error in your browser or using a tool like curl.
steps.hint: Make sure your server is running before testing the route. Check the terminal for any server startup messages.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Add error handling for async routes
steps.instruction: Modify the async route to catch errors using a try-catch block and pass them to the next() function.
steps.hint: Wrap your async code in a try block, and in the catch block, call next(error) to pass the error to your error handling middleware.
steps.expectedOutcome: The async route will now properly catch errors and pass them to Express error handling middleware.
successCriteria: The async route includes a try-catch block that calls next(error) in the catch block.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using both try and catch blocks, and calling next(error) in the catch block.
steps.feedbackWrong: The async route should include a try-catch block that catches errors and passes them to next().

steps.title: Test the complete error handling system
steps.instruction: Test both error routes by visiting them in your browser or using a tool like curl to confirm they're properly caught by your error middleware.
steps.hint: Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3000/error and http://localhost:3000/async-error to see the error responses.
steps.expectedOutcome: Both routes should return JSON error responses with status 500, showing that your error handling middleware is working correctly for synchronous and asynchronous errors.
successCriteria: Both /error and /async-error routes return JSON error responses when visited.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: One route might not be returning the expected error response. Check that both routes are throwing errors and the middleware is correctly registered.
steps.feedbackWrong: Neither route is returning the expected error response. Make sure errors are being thrown in both routes and the error middleware is properly registered.
